newsitem.title: USA: G24 seeks greater say on global economic issues.
newsitem.headline: G24 seeks greater say on global economic issues.

text.p: Developing nations in the Group of 24 said on Sunday that they sought a greater say in global economic affairs and wanted to start a dialogue with the Group of Seven rich nations.

The G24's chairman, Venezuelan Central Bank president Antonio Casas Gonzalez, told a news conference that talks with the G7 should center on issues that affect the interests of both industrialized and developing nations.
"In the near future, these (developing countries) will be the principal part of the world's economy," said Casas after a meeting of G24 ministers at the IMF/World Bank spring meetings.
"We want to have a mechanism by which the G7 will be informed, in one way or another, about the common interests of the G24 and by which we would be able to dialogue with them," he added.
Casas said he had written to U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, who is currently acting as spokesman for the G7 finance ministers, to propose informal talks on a technical level.
The G24's membership includes countries from Africa, Asia and Latin America. Powerhouses like China and South Africa have also attended the group's meetings as observers.
Casas said the G24 ministers would also like to have a meeting of heads of state of developing countries in order to build political support for a dialogue with rich nations.
However, he said that the idea of a G24 summit would require more work before it becomes a concrete proposal.

The G24, which was created 25 years ago as a monetary offshoot of the Group of 77 non-aligned nations, includes Algeria, Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Cote d'Ivoire, Egypt, Ethiopia, Gabon, Ghana, Guatemala, India, Iran, Lebanon, Mexico, Nigeria, Pakistan, Peru, Philippines, Sri Lanka, Syria, Trinidad and Tobago, Venezuela and Zaire.
As usual the G24's communique offered broad comments on the developing nations' views of the world's economic outlook.
"For the fifth year in a row, the developing countries have led in the contributions to world economic growth," they noted.

Regarding the pre-emptive monetary tightening recently undertaken by the United States and Britain, the G24 said it should not be pushed to the point at which it will lead to higher international interest rates.

They also said Europe's pursuit of fiscal consolidation in the run-up to the EMU and the withdrawal of fiscal stimulus in Japan were putting at risk "the growth momentum in large parts of the industrial world, with significant spillover effects on developing country exports and growth."

As for the introduction of a single European currency, the G24 urged the International Monetary Fund to "ensure that the transition to a tripolar currency system proceeds with much closer international coordination to minimize instability in the exchange and capital markets."
